seo.title: South America Semester Abroad | Pacific Discovery
seo.description: Peru, Ecuador & the Galápagos in 10 weeks: Machu Picchu via the Inca Jungle Trail, Spanish lessons, Andean community service, the Amazon and Galápagos snorkeling. Ages 17–22.

route.heading: Your journey at a glance
route.mapAlt: Route map from Cusco, Peru through Ecuador to the Galápagos

phases.label: Week 1–2
phases.text: Live in the Sacred Valley, volunteer on a community project, pick up Spanish and explore the Incan ruins of Pisaq, Ollantaytambo and Moray, then bike and hike your way to Machu Picchu

phases.label: Week 3–4
phases.text: Get to know Cusco through its legends and markets, cook with local ingredients, then head into the mountains on the Llama Pack Trek with the Quishuarani community

phases.label: Week 4
phases.text: Stay with a local family in Llachón, hike and sail by day, island-hop by boat and give back through a community project

phases.label: Week 5–8
phases.text: Ride the Quito TelefériQo, live with a homestay family in Agato, hike the Quilotoa crater rim, zipline and canyon in Baños, raft the Jatunyacu River and go deep into the Cuyabeno Wildlife Reserve

phases.label: Week 9–10
phases.text: Volunteer at Hacienda Tranquila, snorkel Kicker Rock, visit Floreana, hike the Sierra Negra volcano and finish with tunnels, tortoises and flamingos on Isabela

items.title: Guesthouses & lodges
items.body: Hostel style accommodations that are clean and safe.

items.title: Camping nights
items.body: Low camping level. You’ll camp a few nights on this program: a shelter with the Quishuarani community on the llama trek and a night on the river in Tena.

items.title: Homestays
items.body: You'll stay with local communities and share meals with them, in Llachón on Lake Titicaca and in Agato, Ecuador.

itinerary.heading: Week by week
itinerary.note: This is a guide to what you can expect to do on program. The order in which activities occur might vary. Itineraries are subject to change.

weeks.title: Community volunteering & Spanish immersion
weeks.body:
You’ll meet your Program Instructors in Cusco, the heart of the ancient Incan Empire, and head into the Sacred Valley for orientation: getting to know each other, setting the tone for the program and diving into the Peruvian way of life.

This week we explore the Incan ruins of Pisaq, Ollantaytambo and Moray, and start a local service project in Calca, working side by side with the community and learning about their traditions. Afternoon Spanish lessons at two levels mean that whether you’re just starting or looking to level up, you’ll be able to immerse yourself even more in the culture.
weeks.imageAlt: Student painting a bench in bright colours

weeks.title: Biking, zip-lining & exploring Machu Picchu
weeks.location: Calca → Inca Jungle Trail → Machu Picchu, Peru
weeks.body:
After two more days of service and Spanish in Calca, we tour Racchi, set off on a biking tour and visit a coffee farm before a night at a lodge in San Pablo. Then the Inca Jungle Trail: a hike of about 15 km from Huayopata past the Inka Prison to Santa Teresa and its hot springs, and on toward Machu Picchu with a zip line along the way.

From Aguas Calientes we climb Machu Picchu Mountain and tour the archaeological site, then take the train back to Cusco.
weeks.imageAlt: Group sitting in front of Machu Picchu

weeks.title: Culture, cuisine & llamas in the Sacred Valley
weeks.body:
Cusco blends old-world charm with Andean culture: cobbled streets, orange-tiled adobe homes and a towering cathedral. After a free day, a Cusco Legend and Culture Tour takes us to the Qoricancha, the artisans’ neighbourhood of San Blas and the main square. Then we visit the farmers market for the freshest local ingredients and roll up our sleeves for a hands-on cooking class in traditional Peruvian dishes.

In Urubamba we start our second volunteer project with the Llama Pack Project and its resident llamas. The project revives the ancient traditions of llama breeding and use, and supports local communities through environmental education and sustainable rural development. We set off on the Llama Pack Trek and stay with the Quishuarani community.
weeks.imageAlt: Students sitting with local people in traditional dress in the mountains

weeks.title: Llamas & the highest lake on Earth
weeks.body:
We finish our work with the Llama Pack Project and take a day to explore and recover before the bus to Juliaca.

On the shores of Lake Titicaca we stay with local families in the Llachón community. We hike and sail, take a boat trip to the islands and give back through a community project. It’s a chance to unplug from the usual tourist trail and see a part of the world still largely untouched by modern tourism.
weeks.imageAlt: Students trying on traditional clothing with local women

weeks.title: Quito & a truly authentic Ecuadorian experience
weeks.body:
We fly from Juliaca to Quito, ride the TelefériQo for views over the city and spend time exploring.

Then we head to the small village of Agato, high in the Andes, for our homestay. We live alongside local families and contribute to community-driven, sustainable development projects, and spend time with the kids, settling into the rhythms of a culture deeply connected to the earth.
weeks.imageAlt: Student with a local woman and a llama

weeks.title: Agato, markets & the Quilotoa crater
weeks.body:
Our service-learning in Agato continues through most of the week, building real relationships with a community that opens your eyes to a different world.

Then we take the bus through Otavalo, known for its craft market, to Quilotoa, a small village beside a breathtaking crater lake. We hike the crater loop in the morning before taking the bus to Baños.
weeks.imageAlt: Turquoise crater lake surrounded by mountains

weeks.title: Adventure in Baños & rafting into the Amazon
weeks.body:
Baños sits at the foot of the active Tungurahua Volcano. Every morning we have Spanish lessons, and afternoons bring ziplining, the Casa del Árbol hike, salsa lessons, the hot springs and a day of canyoning.

Then we take the bus to Tena on the edge of the Amazon and start a two-day rafting expedition with The River People down the Jatunyacu River, camping by the river for the night.

weeks.title: Chocolate, culture & Cuyabeno wildlife
weeks.body:
Our rafting finishes near Puerto Napo, and we transfer to the Sinchi Warmi Center in Misahualli, an indigenous women’s ecotourism initiative dedicated to sustainability. We join cultural activities and a musical night, hike to a waterfall, and learn how artisanal chocolate is made from scratch.

Then we travel to Lago Agrio and into the Cuyabeno Wildlife Reserve, one of the most biodiverse places on the planet. From a lodge deep in the forest we explore rivers and lakes by canoe with a native guide, watching for wildlife including rare pink and grey freshwater dolphins.
weeks.imageAlt: Group in a canoe on a jungle lagoon

weeks.title: Snorkel with sharks & service on San Cristóbal
weeks.location: Quito → San Cristóbal → Santa Cruz, Galápagos
weeks.body:
We travel back to Quito and fly to San Cristóbal Island, where Darwin first set foot in the Galápagos. Our first project is three days of service at Hacienda Tranquila.

Then it’s time for the water. We snorkel Kicker Rock (León Dormido), a towering rock formation teeming with life, and tour the island’s beaches, looking out for sea turtles, rays, sea lions and marine iguanas, before transferring to Santa Cruz.
weeks.imageAlt: Students trying on giant tortoise shells

weeks.title: Floreana, Isabela & farewell
weeks.body:
A boat takes us to Floreana, where we visit the Peace Asylum and snorkel at Black Beach before continuing to Isabela Island. There we bike to the Wetlands, the Flamingo Lagoon and the Tortoise Centre, hike to the Sierra Negra and Chico volcanoes and snorkel at Los Túneles.

We hold our program wrap on Isabela, reflecting on 10 weeks of exploration, cultural immersion, meaningful projects and friendships, then return to Santa Cruz and fly home from Baltra.
weeks.imageAlt: Group standing on a lava arch above the water

day.heading: What a typical day looks like

notes.title: Free time
notes.body: Each week there is some designated free time to catch up on email and laundry, rest and explore with others in the group.

notes.title: Phones & wifi
notes.body: We encourage flight mode so you stay present. Wifi is available where we stay in cities and towns.

notes.title: Fitness needed
notes.body: High activity level. Be ready for the Inca Jungle Trail, the Llama Pack Trek, rafting and physical work on volunteer projects.

items.title: Spanish immersion
items.body: Improve your conversational Spanish wherever you're starting from. Lessons run at two levels, so beginners and confident speakers both move forward. Classes start in the Sacred Valley in week one and run daily again in Baños. Homestays and community projects give you the chance to use it every day.

items.title: Optional college credit
items.body: Earn college credit through the University of Montana. 529 education funds can be used to pay for your credits and your Pacific Discovery program tuition.

safety.heading: For parents: how we keep students safe

items.title: 24/7 Emergency Line
items.body: Parents, students and instructors can reach a real person at any hour. Every call is logged and passed to our on-call staff member by phone.

items.title: Wilderness First Aid & Live Risk Assessment
items.body: All our instructors hold Wilderness First Aid (WFA) certification and have extensive training in group leadership and risk management.

items.title: Accredited Safety Systems
items.body: Our safety systems are assessed and accredited by the Gap Year Association (USA), Year Out Group (UK) and OutdoorsMark (NZ). Students on Go Overseas voted us one of the top gap year providers for safety.

items.title: Insurance & Health
items.body: Comprehensive travel insurance is required, covering medical costs and emergency evacuation. Check vaccinations with your doctor, and pack a first-aid kit and any personal medication. Our instructors can't legally give students any medication.

faq.heading: Questions we get about this program

items.q: Do I need to speak Spanish?
items.a: No. Lessons run at two levels, so complete beginners and people looking to level up both get something out of them.

items.q: How fit do I need to be?
items.a: The program suits anyone of average fitness. You don't need experience with any of the activities, but be ready to try hiking, biking, rafting and kayaking. Volunteer projects also involve some physical work, such as trail building, tree planting or painting.

items.q: How hard is the Inca Jungle Trail?
items.a: It combines biking, a hike of about 15 km to Santa Teresa, hot springs and a zip line on the way to Machu Picchu, where we climb Machu Picchu Mountain.
A mix of clean, comfortable hostels and lodges, a few camping nights, and homestays with local families in Llachón and Agato.

Tuition covers all in-country transport, accommodation, meals, and the activities and entry fees in the itinerary. It doesn't cover international or internal flights, visas, travel insurance, spending money, optional college credit or optional activities.

items.q: How much spending money should I bring?
items.a: About $100 a week for snacks, laundry, personal shopping and optional activities. It varies from student to student.

items.q: Can I stay in touch with home?
items.a: Yes. We encourage keeping phones on flight mode so you stay present, and wifi is available where we stay in cities and towns. There will also be a photo album that students and instructors can upload photos and video to, so parents and caregivers can stay up to date.

items.q: Do I need a passport or visa?
items.a: Your passport must be valid for more than 6 months after the program ends. All the information you need in regard to visas will be available in your student portal.
